# Emitting Other Abstractions

`[Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Embedded]` works on any type kind: enum, class, struct, record, or interface. You get
a `SourceText` class for it, which is how your generator ships shared types into consuming projects.

## Example: an enum

```csharp
namespace MyGenerator;

[Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Embedded]
internal enum ServiceLifetime
{
    Transient,
    Scoped,
    Singleton,
}
```

One file comes out, `ServiceLifetimeSourceText`:

```csharp
// <auto-generated/>
#nullable enable
#pragma warning disable 0618, 1591, 8019

namespace MyGenerator;

[global::Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Embedded]
[global::System.CodeDom.Compiler.GeneratedCode("ZCrew.Extensions.CodeAnalysis.CSharp", "0.0.0.0")]
internal static partial class ServiceLifetimeSourceText
{
    public static readonly global::Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Text.SourceText SourceText =
        global::Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Text.SourceText.From(
        """
        namespace MyGenerator;

        [Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Embedded]
        internal enum ServiceLifetime
        {
            Transient,
            Scoped,
            Singleton,
        }

        """,
        global::System.Text.Encoding.UTF8
    );

    public static void AddServiceLifetimeDefinition(
        this global::Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.IncrementalGeneratorPostInitializationContext context)
    {
        context.AddSource("MyGenerator.ServiceLifetimeSourceText.g.cs", SourceText);
    }
}
```

So you get the type's source as a `SourceText` field and an `Add{TypeName}Definition()` extension that emits it
under the right hint name. Naming follows `{TypeName}SourceText`, and generic types get an arity suffix, so
`Box<T>` gives you `BoxSourceText_1` and `AddBox_1_Definition()`.

Everything is `global::`-qualified because the output lands in your namespace with no `using` directives.

> Only attributes get the parsing code (the `{Name}Data` record and the `TryGet{Name}Data` / `For{Name}Data`
> extensions). Other types stop at the `SourceText` file.

> The captured text is the whole source file, not just the marked type. Give each embedded type its own file so
> nothing unrelated travels with it.

## Emitting it

### From PostInitializationOutput

Use this when the type should always be emitted:

```csharp
public void Initialize(IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext context)
{
    context.RegisterPostInitializationOutput(static context =>
    {
        context.AddEmbeddedAttributeDefinition();
        context.AddServiceLifetimeDefinition();
    });
}
```

`AddEmbeddedAttributeDefinition()` emits `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.EmbeddedAttribute`, which the embedded type's
own source refers to.

### From RegisterSourceOutput

Use this when it depends on pipeline data:

```csharp
context.RegisterSourceOutput(someProvider, static (context, data) =>
{
    if (data.NeedsLifetimeEnum)
    {
        context.AddSource("ServiceLifetime.g.cs", ServiceLifetimeSourceText.SourceText);
    }
});
```

## Other type kinds

```csharp
// a marker interface
[Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Embedded]
internal interface IGeneratedService { }

// a base class
[Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Embedded]
internal abstract class GeneratedServiceBase
{
    public abstract string Name { get; }
}

// a record struct
[Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Embedded]
internal readonly record struct ServiceDescriptor(string Name, Type ServiceType);
```

Each one gets its own `{TypeName}SourceText` class.

## Tips

- Keep embedded types self-contained. They're emitted as source into someone else's project, so they can't
  depend on types that won't be there.
- Watch out for embedded types referencing each other. If A references B, both have to be embedded and both
  have to be emitted.
- Keep them `internal`. They're an implementation detail of your generator, and `public` leaks them into the
  consuming project's API.
